records.targetEnglish: The meaning is this: just as there are destructive forces within the creation of the world as a whole, so within the individual there are forces that seek to lead him into sin. At the creation of the world, the accusers said, “What is man, that You remember him?” (Psalms 8:5), and desired the world’s destruction. Correspondingly, within the individual there is the power of the inclination that seeks to remove him from the world. When a person overcomes the inclination and breaks this destructive power, he also subdues the accusation above, until he makes himself like the Temple, with Hashem dwelling within him. This is what the holy Zohar says there: “The Temple below stands in the likeness of the Temple above.” By making himself a Temple—that is, by subduing the evil force within him, so that Hashem dwells in him—all the accusers above are subdued, and the world is sweetened. This is the teaching (Avot 2:4), “Nullify your will before His will, so that He will nullify the will of others before your will”: the will of the accusers, the destructive forces. Prayer therefore needs to be in a house, that is, from a place of constriction: without spreading out into the benefits of this world, but held within limits for the honor of Heaven. It is like the shofar sounding from a narrow place (Zohar, Beshalach 60a), a vessel that confines the sound rather than letting it spread without measure. So too, all a person’s prayers and desires must come from a place of constriction, without unbounded expansion. Our father Yitzchak was different: his distinguishing quality was sowing, and he surrendered himself entirely to Hashem. He saw explicitly that everything came from Hashem, and all his actions were directed toward the explicit manifestation of the honor of Heaven. He therefore prayed in the field, meaning that in every expansion of his activity he saw the honor of Heaven.

records.targetEnglish: That [repentance] lengthens a person’s years comes through the unfolding of the level of Yaakov our father, of blessed memory. Chizkiyahu attained this through the extension of his life—“I will add to your days,” and so forth—when his repentance was aroused so powerfully that it broke through all the restrictions, decrees, and limits upon his life, the command “Thus far shall you come,” reaching instead Yaakov’s inheritance without boundaries. That is why Yaakov did not die: death comes through the limit that the Creator sets to human life; where there are no boundaries, death does not apply. His death was only in this world, to outward appearance. As they said (Taanit 5b), “I interpret a verse,” and “He compares him to his descendants”: that is, I expound Scripture, for derash grasps the depth hidden from the plain meaning. Knowledge of the matter in its truth is the derash concealed within the written text that is revealed to everyone. The meaning of his life is “He compares him to his descendants”: simply, the life in his descendants is his own life, for the collective root of the souls of every generation is the soul of Yaakov our father, of blessed memory.
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok reports a teaching that the mode of revelation in Scripture corresponds to the mode of revelation in the world: Yaakov’s continuing life is discerned through derash, although his burial remains visible at the level of ordinary observation.
records.explanation: This is Rav Tzadok’s explicit explanation of the same response, “I interpret a verse.” It distinguishes the outwardly visible written account from the inner reality disclosed by derash and explains Yaakov’s continuing life through the living generations rooted in his soul. That distinction supplies the logic for the argument in Kedushat Shabbat: the patriarchs’ Shabbat could be real while still appearing in Scripture and in history only through hints. The passage corroborates and explains the teaching; it does not identify the unnamed person from whom Rav Tzadok heard it.

records.targetEnglish: This is what the holy Zohar explains here: “Come and see: Yaakov held fast to the Tree of Life, in which there is never death; all life is brought to completion in it, and it gives life to all who hold fast to it,” and so forth. Since he sees that Hashem is not affected by any particular attribute, even the inanimate realm is not fixed and bound by nature: since Hashem created it, it can consequently be refined. The appearance that the inanimate realm is severed from life comes only from Hashem’s having created the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil in the world. From that perspective, one does not see how it continually praises Hashem; in truth, however, the earth too is full of His kindness. Therefore Yaakov our father did not die, as the Sages said in the Gemara, “Yaakov our father did not die,” and as the holy Zohar concludes here. Death is concealment from the human perspective; one who is attached to the Tree of Life sees that a soul of Israel is alive and attached to the root of life. The holy Zohar concludes: “When did he die? At the time of which it is written, ‘He gathered his feet into the bed,’ as it says, ‘Behold, his bed, which is Solomon’s.’ For concerning this bed it is written, ‘Her feet descend to death’ (Proverbs 5:5). Therefore it is written, ‘He gathered his feet into the bed’; then, ‘He expired and was gathered to his people,’” and so forth. A bed alludes to the lower level, which conceals the lower reaches of the higher levels, so that it is not seen how Hashem lives and directs this world.
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok reports a teaching that the mode of revelation in Scripture corresponds to the mode of revelation in the world: Yaakov’s continuing life is discerned through derash, although his burial remains visible at the level of ordinary observation.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains how the two descriptions—Yaakov’s death and his uninterrupted life—can stand together. The lower level conceals the Divine life that one attached to the Tree of Life perceives. This gives content to Rav Tzadok’s claim that only those who probe the inner meaning recognized what was not manifest to every observer. It is a later Radzin explanation of the distinction, not evidence identifying the original speaker of Rav Tzadok’s “I heard.”

records.targetEnglish: And so I heard from my master and teacher, of blessed memory, of Izhbitz, an explanation of the verse “You were rebellious with the Lord.” It should have said “against the Lord”; rather, the meaning is that, after they repent out of love—when deliberate sins become merits—God will clarify that their rebellion too was “with the Lord,” and that these matters issued from Him. This means that God will clarify “If your sins should be like these years,” which have been arranged and have come since the six days of Creation, as stated in Shabbat 89b. For this is the order of Creation: first darkness and afterward light; there is no light except that which emerges from darkness. This is “hovering over the surface of the water”: through the merit of repentance, which is compared to water, as it says, “Pour out your heart like water.” Water represents kindness and love; therefore they said that water signifies Torah. Repentance is like water when it comes from love; then the darkness becomes very good.
records.explanation: This passage supplies an explicit attribution for the otherwise unnamed “I heard”: Rav Tzadok identifies his teacher of Izhbitz while repeating the same verse and interpretation. It also states a condition that is compressed in Kedushat Shabbat: the disclosure comes after repentance from love. The enduring inner bond therefore grounds the possibility of return; the passage does not describe rebellion itself as a consciously meritorious act. Its movement from darkness to light explains how Shabbat’s inward holiness can remain present even when it is concealed by sin.

records.targetEnglish: This is the statement of Zophar the Naamathite: “The rejoicing of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite lasts but a moment … He swallowed wealth and will vomit it up” (Job 20). That is, no lasting share remains within him. Although he swallowed wealth—because at that time it was necessary that, through his strength and resources, he carry out some mission serving God’s will—nevertheless, since it was not done with his awareness and willingness, but merely came about through him, nothing of it will remain within him: “He will vomit it up, and God will dispossess his belly of it.” As the passage concludes, “He will not see streams, rivers flowing with honey and butter.” Honey and milk allude to the good end that is destined, the good recompense for those who serve God and do His will. But since it is not done with his willingness and awareness, and instead is brought about through him without his awareness, he will not see himself enjoying the good destined for those who knowingly do the Creator’s will. In truth, all his rebellion and destruction occur only within the bounded scope of his own grasp and understanding; all the damage he does is only to himself, for God’s will is fulfilled even through him, while he, in his own mind, persists in defiance and rebellion. As stated in the introduction to Tikkunei HaZohar (2a), “From his side, a male servant and a maidservant rule over the world.” In truth, however, the sinner does not damage God’s governance; only “from his side” does he damage and destroy—that is, within the bounded scope of his understanding and grasp, he sees that he has caused destruction in the world. As it says, “He has corrupted himself” (Deuteronomy 32:5), which Onkelos translates: “They have brought destruction upon themselves, not upon Him.”
records.explanation: R. Gershon Henoch Leiner gives the distinction needed to read the phrase “with the Lord” precisely. Divine purpose may be fulfilled through an act whose human intention remains rebellious; the unwilling instrument does not thereby acquire the merit or reward of willing service. This clarifies how Rav Tzadok can affirm an unsevered divine bond without erasing the moral meaning of sin. This is a developed Radzin parallel, not an identification of the person from whom Rav Tzadok heard the teaching. The annotated English edition’s notes 419 and 421 drew attention to this distinction; the quotation here is a new translation of the author’s Hebrew paragraph, not a quotation of those modern notes.

records.themeTitle: Jesse’s sinlessness and the remaining trace of the serpent
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok refers elsewhere for the distinction between having committed no personal sin and having removed the inherited root of bodily desire. That distinction explains why the second tablets and the restored divine presence remained concealed.
records.originHebrew: כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר בְּיִשַׁי שֶׁעָלָיו דָּרְשׁוּ בְּיִחוּד שֶׁנִּקְרָא "נָחָשׁ" (שְׁמוּאֵל ב י״ז:כ״ה; שַׁבָּת נה:) עַל שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ. הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיָה בוֹ רַק הַשְׁאָרַת רְשִׁימוּ מֵהַזּוּהֲמָא שֶׁפָּסְקָה, שֶׁלֹּא נִמְחֲקָה לְגַמְרֵי עֲדַיִן בְּלוּחוֹת אַחֲרוֹנוֹת שֶׁהָיוּ בְּצִנְעָא וְלֹא בְּפִרְסוּם;
records.originEnglish: As I have written elsewhere concerning Jesse, about whom they specifically expounded that he was called “the serpent” (II Samuel 17:25; Shabbat 55b), because he died through the serpent’s instigation. records.targetEnglish: This is what our Sages said (Shabbat 146a): “The impurity ceased in Israel, who stood at Mount Sinai.” The meaning is that the impurity the serpent introduced, as we have explained elsewhere, is desire—as in the Sages’ expression, “When the serpent came,” and so forth. Likewise, I have written elsewhere about what our Sages said (Shabbat 55b) concerning Jesse, who died through the serpent’s instigation. In Midrash Tehillim, on the verse “In iniquity I was formed” (Psalm 51:7), they interpret it as “in full iniquity”: even the most pious of the pious intends only his own pleasure. This is Jesse, David’s father, and this is “the serpent’s instigation.” This is an inborn deficiency in everyone born of woman among Eve’s descendants, and no personal effort can remedy it, even for the most pious of the pious. [This is why death results from the serpent’s instigation, as stated above: death is attachment to bodily enjoyment, which lasts only for a time. As I have written elsewhere on this, death comes from desire, while eternal life comes from its opposite—Torah, which is the opposite of desire; this is not the place to elaborate.] Rather, it is as our Sages said (Yoma 85b): “Who purifies you? The Holy One, blessed be He.” Impurity everywhere denotes desire, as I have written elsewhere, and purification from it is accomplished by the Holy One, blessed be He.
records.explanation: This is a precise expansion of the deferred point: Jesse can be free of personal transgression and still retain the inherited impulse toward self-directed bodily pleasure. Rav Tzadok identifies that residual impulse with the serpent’s impurity and explains why its final purification requires God’s action. In Kedushat Shabbat, this distinguishes the genuine inward purification associated with Sinai from the remaining trace that prevented its full public manifestation after the calf. The connection is supported by the shared Jesse–serpent argument; it does not establish that this particular paragraph was the single location Rav Tzadok had in mind when he wrote “elsewhere.”

records.themeTitle: The Jordan, the liver, and the transformation of anger
records.themeSummary: The received correspondence places anger within the relation of the world to the human soul. These passages explain both how possessive anger is overcome and why holy severity must be distinguished from it.

records.targetEnglish: This is the meaning of “The Lord said to me: You shall not cross this Jordan.” Since [Moses’ task] had been completed, all his service had been brought into the whole community of Israel. Consequently, had he crossed the Jordan, the quality of anger would have been entirely abolished from the world. For the Jordan alludes to anger, as stated in the Talmud (Nedarim 22b): “At that time we had not crossed the Jordan.” And as stated [in Sefer Yetzirah], “The Jordan in the world, the liver in the soul.” That is, had he crossed the Jordan, he would have shown that there is no [unholy] anger in Israel; when we sometimes see anger among Israel, it is entirely the righteous ardor of Torah scholars. God told him, “You shall not cross this Jordan”: for the present, the quality of anger must necessarily exist in the world. Had it been entirely abolished from the world, there would be no scope for divine service, for the root of anger is idolatry. If a person recognized that “the earth and all it contains belong to the Lord,” he would not become angry over anything. As my grandfather and teacher, of blessed memory, illustrated: a person who enters his friend’s house will not become angry if things there are not arranged in the order that he wants. Likewise, if a person recognized that “the earth and all it contains belong to the Lord,” he would not become angry over anything. Anger principally arises because a person does not recognize that God is the owner of the world; he imagines that it is his own. Consequently, when things do not proceed in the order he wants, he becomes angry. If the quality of anger were abolished, that would indicate that a person constantly recognized that “the earth and all it contains belong to the Lord,” and that God is the owner of the entire world. Then there would be no scope for divine service; yet God desires, as it were, Israel’s service in this world.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef preserves the exact Jordan–liver correspondence and explains its spiritual mechanism: possessive anger grows from imagining that the world is one’s own. Moses’ crossing would have made divine ownership so evident that this form of anger could no longer persist. The distinction between that anger and the righteous ardor of Torah scholars directly illuminates Rav Tzadok’s next words, “there are holy judgments.” This is an independent Radzin parallel; it does not identify Rav Tzadok’s unnamed transmitter. The bracketed mention of Sefer Yetzirah translates Tiferet Yosef’s own parenthetical citation, whose precise location has not been established here.

records.targetEnglish: God also created this matter for laughter, as it says, “This Leviathan You formed to play with” (Psalm 104:26) [and it is among the fish]. See the chapter HaSefinah (Bava Batra 74b), that the Jordan rolls down and descends into its mouth. This means, as I have received, that the Jordan in the world is like the liver in the soul. A support for this is the Gemara’s wording (Bekhorot 55a), which juxtaposes “the chief source of the Jordan, etc.” and “the chief source of blood is the liver”; see there. From it comes the power of anger, corresponding to “the liver becomes angry” (Berakhot 61b). Therefore they said (Nedarim 22a), concerning “The Lord will give you there an angry heart” (Deuteronomy 28:65): they had not crossed the Jordan; see there. Laughter is the opposite of anger. This is why laughter was created in the world: to dispel an angry heart and allay it through laughter. Therefore the Jordan rushes into the mouth of Leviathan (Job 40:23), to be consumed in its mouth. All of this is within holiness, for the Jordan too belongs to the Land of Israel and the holy land.
records.explanation: Rav Tzadok repeats both the received correspondence and the same juxtaposition in Bekhorot, then develops what Kedushat Shabbat leaves compressed: the capacity for holy laughter counteracts the angry heart. The image of the Jordan entering Leviathan is read as anger being absorbed and quieted within holiness. This clarifies why the original paragraph distinguishes corrupt anger from holy judgment, rather than treating the Jordan or the liver as inherently evil. The parallel confirms Rav Tzadok’s own use of the teaching; it still does not name the teacher from whom he received it.

records.themeTitle: Nachshon and the “very great blow” at Kivrot HaTaavah
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok reports a received teaching that Nachshon died at Kivrot HaTaavah. Mei HaShiloach gives the same identification and sets out the textual reasoning, while explicitly presenting the identification as an inference.
records.originHebrew: וְקִבַּלְתִּי מִמִּי שֶׁנִּגְלָה לוֹ מִסּוֹד ה' לִירֵאָיו: דְּשָׁם מֵת נַחְשׁוֹן, וְשֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר "מַכָּה רַבָּה" (בַּמִּדְבָּר י״א:ל״ג). וְנִרְאֶה דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא נַחְשׁוֹן גַּם כֵּן עַל שֵׁם נָחָשׁ כְּיִשַׁי, כִּי הָיָה בוֹ רַק הָרוֹשֶׁם דְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ.
records.originEnglish: And I received from someone to whom something of “the secret of the Lord belongs to those who fear Him” had been revealed: that Nachshon died there, and that the words “a great blow” (Numbers 11:33) refer to this. It appears that this is why Nachshon too was named for the serpent, like Jesse, for there remained in him only the trace of the serpent’s instigation.

records.targetHebrew: הַבָּשָׂר עוֹדֶנּוּ בֵּין שִׁנֵּיהֶם טֶרֶם יִכָּרֵת וְגוֹ' וַיַּךְ ה' בָּעָם מַכָּה רַבָּה מְאֹד וְגוֹ'. וְלֹא נֶאֱמַר וַיָּמָת עַם רָב רַק "מַכָּה רַבָּה מְאֹד" שֶׁמִּלָּשׁוֹן זֶה מַשְׁמַע שֶׁנִּלְקַח מֵהֶם נֶפֶשׁ יָקָר לִמְאֹד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ שֶׁכָּתוּב (ש"ב כ"ד,ט"ז) "וַיֹּאמֶר לַמַּלְאָךְ הַמַּשְׁחִית בָּעָם רָב" וְאִיתָא עַל זֶה בַּגְּמָרָא (ברכות ס"ב:) אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר לֵיהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַמַּלְאָךְ טוֹל לִי רַב שֶׁבָּהֶם שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ לִיפָּרַע מֵהֶם כַּמָּה חוֹבוֹת בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה מֵת אֲבִישַׁי בֶּן צְרוּיָה שֶׁשָּׁקוּל כְּרוּבָּהּ שֶׁל סַנְהֶדְרִין, וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע בְּכָאן שֶׁמֵּת בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה נֶפֶשׁ יָקָר, וְנִרְאֶה שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה נַחְשׁוֹן בֶּן עַמִּינָדָב, וְסֶמֶךְ לָזֶה מִזה"ק (בהעלותך קנ"ו.) הָא אֲנָא פְּגִימָא וְאַהֲרֹן פָּגִים וְנַחְשׁוֹן בֶּן עַמִּינָדָב פָּגִים, כִּי נַחְשׁוֹן הָיָה דְּרוֹעָא שְׂמָאלָא כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזה"ק (ואתחנן ר"ס:) וּמִיתַת מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן נִכְתַּב בַּתּוֹרָה וּמִיתַת נַחְשׁוֹן לֹא נִכְתַּב.
records.targetEnglish: “The meat was still between their teeth, before it was cut off … and the Lord struck the people with a very great blow,” and so forth. It does not say, “Many people died,” but “a very great blow”; this wording implies that a very precious soul was taken from them. Similarly, we find it written, “He said to the angel destroying the people: Rav” (II Samuel 24:16). The Gemara comments on this (Berakhot 62b): Rabbi Elazar said that the Holy One, blessed be He, told the angel, “Take for Me the great one among them, through whom many of their debts can be exacted.” At that moment Avishai son of Tzeruyah died; he was equivalent to a majority of the Sanhedrin. Likewise, the wording here implies that a precious soul died at that time, and it appears that this was Nachshon son of Amminadav. A support for this is the holy Zohar (Beha’alotcha 156a): “Behold, I am impaired, Aaron is impaired, and Nachshon son of Amminadav is impaired.” For Nachshon was the left arm, as stated in the holy Zohar (Va’etchanan 260b). The deaths of Moses and Aaron are written in the Torah, while the death of Nachshon is not written.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach supplies the precise missing exposition: “great” is read as the loss of an especially great person, by analogy with the Talmud’s interpretation of “rav” concerning Avishai. It then proposes Nachshon and cites the Zohar as support. This is much closer than a general passage about desire or the wilderness: it matches the person, event, and verse in Rav Tzadok’s received teaching. The translation preserves “it appears,” because the printed Ishbitz passage presents the identification as an inference. It corroborates the teaching’s presence in Ishbitz literature without proving the identity of Rav Tzadok’s unnamed transmitter. Rav Tzadok’s further connection between Nachshon’s name and the serpent is his ensuing development, not part of this quoted entry.
records.translationProvenance: New editorial English translation of the complete Hebrew entry from Sefaria’s Vocalized Edition of Mei HaShiloach; the complete Beha’alotcha section and complete originating Kedushat Shabbat 6 were read. The tentative ונראה is preserved, and explanation is separate from quotation.

records.themeTitle: The same teaching: Shabbat’s holiness is already fixed
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok recalls his teacher’s distinction between the sanctification of festivals by Israel and the already established holiness of Shabbat. He preserves this same teaching in the Mishpatim discourses.
records.originHebrew: וּנְהִירְנָא דְּשָׁמַעְתִּי מִמּוֹרִי הַקָּדוֹשׁ זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה, שֶׁאָמַר בְּיִשּׁוּב תְּמִיהַת תּוֹסָפוֹת דְּשַׁבָּת הַנִּזְכֶּרֶת לְעֵיל, דִּלְדַעְתּוֹ בְּשַׁבָּת לֵיכָּא עֲשֵׂה! וְנָתַן טַעַם לִדְבָרָיו: דְּרַק יוֹם טוֹב דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשֵׁי לֵיהּ, שַׁיָּיךְ גַּבֵּיהּ צִיוּוּי מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה עַל הַשְּׁבִיתָה; אֲבָל שַׁבָּת דִּקְבִיעָא וְקַיָּימָא, לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ גַּבֵּיהּ צִיוּוּי מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה; עַד כָּאן תּוֹרֶף דְּבָרָיו כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁיָּצְאוּ מִפִּיו הַקָּדוֹשׁ בְּקִיצּוּר נִמְרָץ וְלֹא בֵּיאֵר יוֹתֵר.
records.originEnglish: I remember hearing from my holy teacher, of blessed memory, that, in resolving the question of Tosafot in Shabbat mentioned above, he said that in his opinion there is no positive commandment of Shabbat rest. He explained: Only regarding a festival, which Israel sanctifies, is a positive commandment of resting applicable; regarding Shabbat, whose sanctity is fixed and established, a positive commandment of this kind is not applicable. This is the substance of his words, as they came from his holy mouth with extreme brevity; he explained no further.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 4
records.targetHebrew: וְהִנֵּה הַשֵּׁם נִצָּב עָלָיו. זֶה הַפָּסוּק בְּעַצְמוֹ הוּא בְּרָכָה, וּבֵיאֵר זֶה כְּמוֹ שֶׁקְּדוּשַּׁת שַׁבָּת הִיא קָבוּעַ וְקַיְימָא בְּלִי שׁוּם הַקְדָּשָׁה וְאִתְעֲרוּתָא מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל רַק מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ הוּא קָדוֹשׁ, לֹא כְּיָמִים טוֹבִים שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשִׁין אוֹתָם, כָּךְ הוּא קְדוּשַּׁת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ כִּקְדוּשַּׁת שַׁבָּת, שֶׁקָּדוֹשׁ מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לְשׁוּם אִתְעֲרוּתָא, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נֶאֱמַר "עוֹמֵד עָלָיו" רַק "נִצָּב" כִּי "עוֹמֵד" מַשְׁמַע שֶׁעַתָּה עוֹמֵד עָלָיו וְלֹא מִקֹּדֶם וְהַיְינוּ מִכֹּחַ אִתְעֲרוּתָא דִּילֵיהּ, אֲבָל "נִצָּב" הַיְינוּ שֶׁתָּמִיד מְקֻשָּׁר עִמּוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: “And behold, Hashem stood over him.” This verse is itself a blessing. He explained it as follows: just as the holiness of Shabbat is fixed and enduring without any sanctification or awakening on Israel’s part, being holy solely from Hashem Himself—unlike the festivals, which Israel sanctifies—so the holiness of Yaakov our father resembles the holiness of Shabbat. He is holy from Hashem’s side and requires no awakening [on his part]. Therefore it does not say “standing [omed] over him” but “stationed [nitzav]”: “omed” would mean that He stands over him now but did not previously, namely, as a result of [Yaakov’s] awakening; “nitzav” means that He is always bound with him.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach states the precise distinction on which the remembered teaching rests: Shabbat’s holiness is established by Hashem before any initiative from Israel, whereas festivals involve Israel’s sanctification. Its application to Yaakov explains what “fixed and enduring” means—a Divine bond that precedes the person’s awakening. This illuminates the premise of the teacher’s brief explanation. The passage does not itself state the disputed halakhic conclusion that Shabbat lacks an additional positive commandment of rest, and it does not establish the wording or occasion of the oral report. Rav Tzadok’s explicit parallel in Peri Tzadik, Mishpatim 6:2, already cited at this location, preserves that legal proposal together with the differing approach of Rambam and Tosafot.
records.translationProvenance: New editorial translation checked directly against the complete preferred canonical Hebrew paragraph in the reader corpus. Its adjacent teachings, Vayetzei 3 and 5, were read. Brackets clarify the subject of the awakening and preserve the Hebrew distinction between omed and nitzav. The complete originating Shvitat Shabbat 1 was read, including Rav Tzadok’s qualifications and competing halakhic views. This is a conceptual parallel, not a claimed identification of the specific oral report.

records.themeTitle: The kohen’s sanctity comes from the sanctity of Israel
records.themeSummary: The oral teaching joins two details: the absence of a step between the courts according to the first opinion in Middot, and the absence of a daily blessing “Who made me a kohen.” Rav Tzadok records the conversation at greater length in Emor.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן שָׁמַעְתִּי: דְּעַל כֵּן אֵין מַעֲלוֹת מֵעֶזְרַת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְעֶזְרַת כֹּהֲנִים לְתַנָּא קַמָּא דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב בְּמִדּוֹת (פֶּרֶק ב מִשְׁנָה ו), דְּמַה שֶּׁנִּבְחֲרוּ בִּכְהֻנָּה אֵינוֹ מִצַּד מַעֲלָה יְתֵירָה שֶׁבָּהֶם עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל. וְכֵן דְּמִטַּעַם זֶה אֵין הַכֹּהֵן מְבָרֵךְ "שֶׁעָשַׂנִי כֹּהֵן".
records.originEnglish: I also heard that this is why, according to the first tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov in Middot (2:6), there are no steps from the Court of Israel to the Court of the Priests: their selection for the priesthood is not due to an additional superiority over Israel. For this same reason, the kohen does not recite the blessing “Who made me a kohen.”
records.targetHebrew: וכדברי רה"ק זצ"ל ששאל מדוע אין הכהנים מברכין בכל יום שעשאני כהן, והשיבותי הלוא גם ישראל אינם מברכין שעשאני ישראל רק שלא עשאני גוי ועבד וגם אין מברכין שעשאני איש רק שלא עשאני אשה (ועי' באו"ח סי' מ"ו בטו"ז ומג"א שם), והטעם שאין לברך שעשאני ישראל כי האדם עדיין הוא תחת הבחירה ובשם ישראל יכונה זה שבחור בטוב ומי יודע אם יכול לעמוד בבחירתו ולכן אינם מברכין רק שלא עשאני גוי ועבד ועכ"פ ניתן תחת הבחירה לבחור בטוב מחמת שאינו גוי ועבד, וכן שלא עשאני אשה ובבחירתו לקיים כל המצות שהאיש מצווה יתר על האשה וכן בכהן לא שייך לברך שעשאני כהן כי גם כן הבחירה בידו להכניס הקדושה בלבו וגם צריך שלא לחלל את כהונתו, ושלא עשאני ישראל בודאי ל"ש לברך דגם הם ישראל גם כן וח"ו לומר כן. והסכים לדברי שהוא תי' אמתי, והוא זצ"ל אמר שלדעתו כהנים אין בהם מעלה באמת דכל הקדושה שבהם מכח ישראל שמכניסין בהם קדושה והוסיף ואמר שזה הוא הפלוגתא בין התנאים במשנה (פ"ב דמדות מ"ו) ראשי פספסין מבדילין בין עזרת ישראל לעזרת כהנים היינו שלא היה מעלות בין עזרת ישראל לעזרת כהנים רק פספסין מבדילין ור' אליעזר בן יעקב אומר מעלה היתה וגבוה אמה, ומרומז דהת"ק סובר שאין לכהן שום מעלה על ישראל שקדושת הכהנים הוא מצד קדושת ישראל שקדושת הכהנים הוא מצד קדושת ישראל כמש"כ ממנו יתד ממנו פינה, וראב"י סובר שיש לכהנים צד קדושה יתירה על קדושת ישראל ולזה אמר שהיה שם מעלה אחת, וידוע דבכל הפלוגתות או"א דא"ח ושניהם אמת כי הצד מעלה יתירה שיש לכהנים הוא גם כן מצד קדושת ישראל,
records.targetEnglish: This accords with the words of the holy rabbi, of blessed memory, who asked why the priests do not bless each day, “Who made me a kohen.” I answered: Israelites, too, do not bless “Who made me an Israelite,” but “Who did not make me a gentile or a slave”; nor do they bless “Who made me a man,” but “Who did not make me a woman” (see Orach Chayim 46, Taz and Magen Avraham there). The reason not to bless “Who made me an Israelite” is that a person still has free choice. The name Israel designates one who chooses the good, and who knows whether he will stand firm in his choice? Therefore they bless only “Who did not make me a gentile or a slave”: at least he has been given the choice to choose the good, since he is neither a gentile nor a slave. Likewise, “Who did not make me a woman”: it is in his choice to fulfill all the commandments incumbent on a man beyond those incumbent on a woman. A kohen likewise cannot appropriately bless “Who made me a kohen,” because it is also in his choice to bring holiness into his heart, and he must also refrain from profaning his priesthood. Certainly “Who did not make me an Israelite” is inappropriate, since they, too, are Israelites—Heaven forbid saying such a thing. He agreed that my answer was true. He, of blessed memory, said that in his view priests do not really have superiority, for all their holiness comes from the power of Israel, who bring holiness into them. He added that this is the dispute between the tannaim in the Mishnah (Middot 2:6): “The ends of markers divide the Court of Israel from the Court of the Priests.” That is, there were no steps between the Court of Israel and the Court of the Priests; only markers separated them. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says, “There was a step, a cubit high.” This intimates that the first tanna holds that the kohen has no superiority over Israel, since the holiness of the priests comes from the holiness of Israel—since the holiness of the priests comes from the holiness of Israel—as it is written, “From him the supporting peg, from him the cornerstone.” Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that the priests have an aspect of holiness beyond the holiness of Israel; therefore he says that there was one step. It is known that in all disputes “these and those are the words of the living God,” and both are true: even the aspect of additional superiority that the priests possess comes from the holiness of Israel.
records.explanation: Emor supplies the unusually precise combination of details recalled here: the blessing, the court boundary, and the first tanna’s view. It also preserves Rav Tzadok’s own answer about the responsibility to realize holiness through choice, followed by the holy rabbi’s different explanation. The quotation retains Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov’s raised step and Rav Tzadok’s reconciliation, so the note does not present one architectural opinion as unanimous or erase the distinct priestly service. The wording identifies the speaker only as “the holy rabbi”; this parallel does not by itself establish his personal identity. The repeated Hebrew clause about Israel’s holiness is retained in translation.
records.translationProvenance: New English translation of the exact selected canonical Hebrew, checked against the complete target paragraph and the complete Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 7 argument. Target text also confirmed through the live Kisvei library MCP on 2026-10-21. Abbreviations are expanded in English; explanatory identifications in brackets are editorial. Quotation and explanation remain separate. No identity is assigned to an unnamed oral teacher.

records.themeTitle: From seeing the light to acquiring it in the heart
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes a revelation granted at the Sea from the work that makes it an enduring possession. The parallel accounts explain both the interval of concealment and the human service required within it.
records.originHebrew: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּעִיקַּר הַהִתְגַּלּוּת הָיָה בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף, שֶׁאָמְרוּ: דְּרָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָאָה יְחֶזְקֵאל (מְכִילְתָּא בְּשַׁלַּח); רַק שֶׁהָיָה בִּרְאִיָּה לְבַד וְלֹא בְּקִנְיָן קָבוּעַ בַּלֵּב. וְהַסָּלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ דִּ"בִּרְאִיָּה בְּעָלְמָא קָנֵי" כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ בָּבָא מְצִיעָא (ב:), הַיְינוּ שֶׁבְּדַעַת בְּנֵי אָדָם, כְּשֶׁמַּשִּׂיג הַדָּבָר בִּרְאִיָּה, חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁכְּבָר הִשִּׂיגוֹ וְשֶׁהוּא בְּקִנְיָן; וְהָאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ כֵן, דְּאַחַר כָּךְ בָּאוּ לִרְפִידִים – לְרִפְיוֹן יָדָם מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.), וּמִיָּד בָּא עֲמָלֵק הַמְקַטְרֵג. וְעַל זֶה הֵם יְמֵי הַסְּפִירָה כַּיָּדוּעַ: לְטַהֵר עַצְמֵנוּ מִכָּל זוּהֲמָא, כְּדֵי לִזְכּוֹת לְקַבָּלַת תּוֹרָה בְּשָׁבוּעוֹת; וְאָז בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה זָכוּ לִקְבִיעַת אוֹתוֹ אוֹר בְּקִנְיָן קָבוּעַ בַּלֵּב.
records.originEnglish: I heard that the principal revelation was at the splitting of the Sea, where they said that a maidservant saw what Ezekiel did not see (Mekhilta, Beshalach). Yet this was sight alone, not an acquisition firmly established in the heart. The initial supposition that “one acquires by mere sight,” mentioned at the beginning of Bava Metzia (2b), means that when people apprehend something by seeing it, they think they have already attained and acquired it. In truth it is not so: afterward they came to Rephidim, where their hands weakened in words of Torah (Sanhedrin 106a), and immediately Amalek the accuser came. This is the purpose of the days of counting: to purify ourselves of every impurity so as to merit receiving Torah on Shavuot. At the giving of the Torah, they then merited having that light established as a lasting acquisition in the heart.
records.targetHebrew: וגירסת הגאונים בניסן המליך אות ה' בראי', ובאייר המליך אות ו' בשמיעה, והענין כמו ששמעתי מרה"ק זצוק"ל שבניסן היה רק מחסד ד' והיה התגלות רק לפי שעה בליל יציאת מצרים ואחר כך נעלם. ובקי"ס זכו רק לראי' כמ"ש (מכילתא וזה"ק בשלח) ראתה שפחה על הים וכו' ונעלם מהם גם כן אחר כך האור, וכענין חוזק החסידות בתחלתו. שאמר רבינו ר' בינם זצוק"ל שעז"נ אל תאמר שהימים הראשונים טובים מאלה כי לא מחכמה שאלת ע"ז. שהיא בא רק בשאלה, שמראין לאדם מה שיוכל לקנות על ידי יגיעתו. ובסיון זכו בקנין. ואמר שאייר נברא באות ו' שכ' בשם רב האי גאון ז"ל דהו' מחבר נקרא ו' מלשון ווי העמודים וכן צורת הו' כווי העמודים, וכן תמיד אות ו' מחבר התיבות. וכן חודש אייר מחבר חודש ניסן וחודש סיון שיזכו בסיון בקנין במה שזכו בניסן בראי'. וז"ש בניסן בראי' ובאייר בשמיעה, שהשמיעה קבלה בלב כענין מה שמצינו בגמ' לא שמוע לי כלומר לא ס"ל, וז"ש באייר המליך אות ו' בשמיעה,
records.targetEnglish: The version of the Geonim is: in Nisan He made the letter heh rule over sight, and in Iyar He made the letter vav rule over hearing. The meaning is as I heard from the holy rabbi, of blessed memory: in Nisan it was solely through God’s kindness, and the revelation was only for a time, on the night of the Exodus from Egypt, after which it disappeared. At the splitting of the Sea they attained only sight, as stated in the Mekhilta and the holy Zohar, Beshalach: “A maidservant saw at the Sea,” and so forth. That light, too, subsequently disappeared from them. This resembles the strength of devotion at its beginning. Our master Rabbi Bunim, of blessed memory, said that this is the meaning of “Do not say that the earlier days were better than these, for it is not from wisdom that you have asked about this”: it comes only on loan, when a person is shown what he can acquire through his toil. In Sivan they attained acquisition. He said that Iyar was created with the letter vav. It is written in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, of blessed memory, that the connecting vav is called vav from “the hooks of the pillars”; the shape of vav also resembles those hooks, and the letter vav always joins words. So too, the month of Iyar joins Nisan and Sivan, so that in Sivan they may acquire what they attained in Nisan through sight. This is the meaning of “in Nisan through sight, and in Iyar through hearing”: hearing is acceptance in the heart, as in the Talmudic expression “I have not heard it,” meaning “I do not accept it.” This is the meaning of “in Iyar He made the letter vav rule over hearing.”
records.explanation: This is a close parallel to the oral teaching itself: it repeats the Sea’s temporary vision, the light’s withdrawal, and its acquisition in Sivan. It adds the missing bridge: Iyar and the counting period turn an illumination first shown to a person into an inwardly accepted attainment. The image of a loan explains why the first experience can disappear without proving it false. Rav Tzadok separately names Rabbi Bunim for the interpretation of the “earlier days” verse; the surrounding oral report calls its speaker only “the holy rabbi,” so the note preserves that distinction rather than assigning every sentence to one named teacher. In the continuation here, Rav Tzadok makes this acquisition relative to the light of the Sea; higher levels begin a new cycle of faith, vision, and acquisition.

records.themeTitle: From seeing the light to acquiring it in the heart
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes a revelation granted at the Sea from the work that makes it an enduring possession. The parallel accounts explain both the interval of concealment and the human service required within it.
records.originHebrew: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּעִיקַּר הַהִתְגַּלּוּת הָיָה בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף, שֶׁאָמְרוּ: דְּרָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָאָה יְחֶזְקֵאל (מְכִילְתָּא בְּשַׁלַּח); רַק שֶׁהָיָה בִּרְאִיָּה לְבַד וְלֹא בְּקִנְיָן קָבוּעַ בַּלֵּב. וְהַסָּלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ דִּ"בִּרְאִיָּה בְּעָלְמָא קָנֵי" כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ בָּבָא מְצִיעָא (ב:), הַיְינוּ שֶׁבְּדַעַת בְּנֵי אָדָם, כְּשֶׁמַּשִּׂיג הַדָּבָר בִּרְאִיָּה, חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁכְּבָר הִשִּׂיגוֹ וְשֶׁהוּא בְּקִנְיָן; וְהָאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ כֵן, דְּאַחַר כָּךְ בָּאוּ לִרְפִידִים – לְרִפְיוֹן יָדָם מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.), וּמִיָּד בָּא עֲמָלֵק הַמְקַטְרֵג. וְעַל זֶה הֵם יְמֵי הַסְּפִירָה כַּיָּדוּעַ: לְטַהֵר עַצְמֵנוּ מִכָּל זוּהֲמָא, כְּדֵי לִזְכּוֹת לְקַבָּלַת תּוֹרָה בְּשָׁבוּעוֹת; וְאָז בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה זָכוּ לִקְבִיעַת אוֹתוֹ אוֹר בְּקִנְיָן קָבוּעַ בַּלֵּב.

records.targetEnglish: The matter is this: after the great revelation of light that Israel previously experienced—as the Sages said, “A maidservant saw at the Sea what Ezekiel did not see”—when this clarity afterward disappeared from them, a question and doubt arose in their hearts about their essential attachment. They said: if we are truly attached above, at the root, why has this light been concealed from us? Previously, while they stood at the Sea, the blessed God illuminated for them a very high level, above prayer and service, as stated in the holy Zohar (Beshalach 47b): “And you shall be silent”—certainly silent; do not arouse a word, for it is not needed from you, and so forth. That is, Israel has an attachment above prayer and service. Afterward, “they traveled three days in the wilderness and found no water.” Because of this their hearts fell greatly: perhaps even the high illumination that had previously shone for them was not, Heaven forbid, from the root. Although a person may inquire into this—as stated in Tanna Devei Eliyahu, that a person should know within himself what he is before his Creator—their entire sin was as explained there in the holy Zohar: “Why were they punished? Because they did not act with love, but by putting Him to the test,” and so forth. That is, they turned this inquiry into a test and an action. As stated there in Midrash Rabbah: if we think in our hearts and He knows what we think, we will serve Him; if not, we will rebel against Him, and so forth. In other words: if the blessed God knows what we lack, why does He not supply our lack? This was the entire sin: they should have attributed the deficiency to themselves, as is indeed the case. The blessed God knows well what is in their hearts—that is, what they lack—for “His compassion is upon all His works.” All the obstruction is only from their side. From the blessed God’s side, however, two opposites can indeed coexist in one subject: they are truly attached to the supernal root, and yet from their side they must constantly remain in prayer and service so that there should be no obstruction on their part.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the failure at Rephidim that Rav Tzadok uses as evidence that sight was not yet lasting acquisition. Israel mistook the disappearance of felt clarity for a possible loss of its underlying bond with Hashem. The corrective is to preserve that bond while continuing prayer and service. This gives content to the work between revelation and acquisition: genuine attachment does not remove the need to clear the obstruction on the recipient’s side. It is a developed Radzin parallel, not evidence that this later discourse was the unidentified source Rav Tzadok heard.

records.themeTitle: Amos’s rebuke also carries a promise of restoration
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok says that he heard an interpretation of Amos’s closing passage concerning damage to the covenant. Chanukah records the teaching with its essential consolation: no individual is finally lost.
records.originHebrew: וְשָׁמַעְתִּי דְּפָרָשָׁה זוֹ נֶאֶמְרָה עַל פְּגַם הַבְּרִית, וְהַמֵּבִין יָבִין דְּכָל פְּסוּקֵי אוֹתָהּ פָּרָשָׁה מֵעִנְיָן זֶה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי בֵּיאוּר מִקְצָתָם וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.
records.originEnglish: I heard that this passage was said concerning damage to the covenant. One who understands will understand that all the verses of that passage concern this matter, as I heard explanations of some of them; this is not their place.
records.targetHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי מֵרַבֵּנוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ זְכַר צַדִּיק וְקָדוֹשׁ לִבְרָכָה לְחַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא: דְּפָסוּק "הֲלוֹא כִבְנֵי כֻשִׁיִּים אַתֶּם לִי" מְרַמֵּז עַל בְּנֵי הַנְּעוּרִים שֶׁדָּוֶה לִבָּם עַל שֶׁהֵמָּה מְשֻׁקָּעִים בְּזוֹ הַתַּאֲוָה, וְלָכֵן נִקְרְאוּ "בְּנֵי כֻשִׁיִּים"; וּמְנַחֵם אוֹתָם בָּזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר אַחַר כָּךְ: "כִּי הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה וְגוֹמֵר וְלֹא יִפּוֹל צְרוֹר אָרֶץ", שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ "חֹשֵׁב מַחֲשָׁבוֹת לְבִלְתִּי יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח", שֶׁהַכֹּל יִהְיֶה נִתְקָן בְּעֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.targetEnglish: As I heard from our holy teacher, may the memory of the righteous and holy be a blessing for the life of the World to Come: the verse “Are you not like the children of the Cushites to Me?” alludes to young people whose hearts ache because they are immersed in this desire [the sexual desire under discussion]; therefore they are called “children of the Cushites.” He consoles them with what is said afterward: “For behold, I command … and not a pebble shall fall to the ground.” The blessed God “devises plans so that none of His banished ones shall be banished,” so that everything will be repaired with the help of the blessed God.
records.explanation: This passage records the same interpretive subject and identifies it as a teaching heard from “our holy teacher,” while leaving that teacher unnamed here. Its crucial addition is the movement from Amos 9:7 to 9:9: the rebuke is accompanied by consolation for young people distressed by their conduct. “Not a pebble shall fall” is read as the assurance that no individual will be discarded from the work of restoration. The quotation preserves the author’s figurative use of the biblical wording. The later Mei HaShiloach anthology reproduces this teaching from Peri Tzadik; that compilation is a useful locator, not an independent witness.

records.themeTitle: The deferred explanation follows Amos from sifting to restoration
records.themeSummary: The phrase “I heard explanations of some of them; this is not their place” points to the verses of Amos 9. Vayigash provides a sustained exposition of the sifting, the plowman and reaper, and the raising of David’s fallen sukkah.
records.originHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי בֵּיאוּר מִקְצָתָם וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ. וְעַל כֵּן הִיא הַפְטָרַת פָּרָשַׁת קְדוֹשִׁים, שֶׁהוּא לְגֶדֶר עֶרְוָה, דְּשָׁם אַתָּה מוֹצֵא קְדוּשָּׁה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה כד, ו).
records.originEnglish: As I heard explanations of some of them; this is not their place. Therefore this is the haftarah of the portion Kedoshim, which concerns a boundary against forbidden sexual relations, for there you find holiness (Vayikra Rabbah 24:6).
records.targetHebrew: ואמר הכ' כי הנה אנכי מצוה והנעותי וגו' ולא יפול צרור ארץ. שזה תכלית הגליות שיתבררו כל נפשות ישראל איש מהם לא נעדר שכולם בכלל מש"נ ועמך כולם צדיקים וזש"נ ולא יפול צרור ארץ. ואח"ז נא' הנה ימים באים ונגש חורש זה יהודה וכו' במושך הזרע זה יוסף שמשך זרעו של אביו והורידו למצרים וכו'. שגלות הראשון היה למצרים שהיא ערות הארץ ולשם נמשכו ע"י יוסף שבא ראשונה למצרים. ואי' (שהש"ר פר' ד) יוסף ירד למצרים וגדר עצמו מן הערוה ונגדרו כל הזכרים בזכותו. וז"ש שמשך זרעו של אביו כו' היינו שיתוקנו כולם שיהיו בכלל ועמך כולם וגו' ובאמת נתבררו שם הכל. אך מ"מ הוצרכו עוד לגליות ע"ד מש"נ כי שבע יפול צדיק וקם והוא שיש ז' נפילות שע"י זה יתבררו היטב במדה זו. וזש"נ ביום ההוא אקים את סוכת דוד הנופלת ועל שם זה נקרא משיח בר נפלי כמ"ש (סנהדרין צו סע"ב)
records.targetEnglish: Scripture says, “For behold, I command, and I shall shake … and not a pebble shall fall to the ground.” This is the purpose of the exiles: that all the souls of Israel should be refined, with not one of them missing, so that all are included in “Your people are all righteous.” This is the meaning of “not a pebble shall fall to the ground.” Afterward it says, “Behold, days are coming … and the plowman shall meet”—this is Yehudah—[“the reaper”], and so forth; “the one who draws the seed”—this is Yosef, who drew his father’s offspring and brought them down to Egypt, and so forth. The first exile was to Egypt, “the nakedness of the land,” and they were drawn there through Yosef, who came to Egypt first. It is stated in Shir HaShirim Rabbah, chapter 4: Yosef descended to Egypt and guarded himself against forbidden sexual relations, and all the males guarded themselves in his merit. This is the meaning of “who drew his father’s offspring,” and so forth: that all should be repaired so that they are included in “Your people are all ….” In truth, all were refined there. Nevertheless, further exiles were needed, in the manner of “For a righteous person falls seven times and rises”: there are seven falls through which they are thoroughly refined in this quality. This is the meaning of “On that day I shall raise the fallen sukkah of David.” On this account Mashiach is called Bar Nafli [the son of the fallen], as stated in Sanhedrin 96b.
records.explanation: This supplies an actual sequence of verse interpretations for the discussion deferred here: Amos 9:9 describes sifting without losing a soul; 9:13 joins Yehudah and Yosef and the work of covenantal repair; 9:11 presents the fallen sukkah as destined to rise. The complete Vayigash paragraph begins with an oral teaching about this same Amos passage. Its continuation distinguishes Yosef’s unblemished righteousness from David’s work of repentance: Mashiach brings a thought of repentance into the community, and Rav Tzadok expressly says that forgiveness is not granted “for nothing.” The promised repair therefore includes repentance. The paragraph then turns to Shabbos as a time of repair. The note identifies a documented expansion in Rav Tzadok’s writings; it does not claim to reconstruct every word of the oral explanation he heard.

records.themeTitle: A first occurrence reveals the root of a meaning
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok’s rule that a first scriptural occurrence reveals a word’s root is clarified by his application to sight and the light of Torah, together with his Talmudic precedent concerning the letter tet.
records.originHebrew: וּפַעַם הָרִאשׁוֹן הוּא בִּתְחִלַּת נְבוּאַת שְׁמוּאֵל עַל הַשָּׂגַת הַנְּבִיאִים נֶאֱמַר: "וּדְבַר ה' הָיָה יָקָר בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם" (שְׁמוּאֵל א ג׳:א׳). וְכָל מִלָּה בַּמָּקוֹם שֶׁהוּא נִזְכָּר רִאשׁוֹנָה שָׁם הוּא גִּלּוּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ עִנְיָנָהּ, וְכִמְדוּמֶּה שֶׁקִּבַּלְתִּי כֵּן
records.originEnglish: Its first occurrence is at the beginning of Samuel’s prophecy: concerning prophetic apprehension it says, “The word of the Lord was precious in those days” (I Samuel 3:1). Every word, in the place where it is first mentioned, reveals the root of its meaning; and it seems to me that I received this teaching.
records.targetHebrew: דהראיה עיקרה נבראת לראות בתורה דדברים שבכתב אי אתה רשאי לאומרן בע"פ (גיטין ס':). וראיה ראשונה שנזכר בתורה הוא על האור בפ' וירא הא' את האור כי טוב ובכל מקום במה שנזכר פעם ראשונה בתורה שם הוא שורש הדבר כמו שנאמר (ב"ק נ"ה.) באות ט' שמורה על טובה אף שיש ט' להיפך גם כן רק הואיל ופתח בו הכתוב לטובה תחלה שמבראשית עד וירא א' את האור כי טוב לא כתיב ט'. וכן הראיה גם כן מפני שפתח בו הכתוב תחלה אצל האור כנ"ל הוא עיקר שורש הראי' והאור שבפ' זה מוסב על אור תורה כמ"ש (ב"ר פ' ג') ה' פעמים אורה בפ' יהי אור כנגד ה' חומשי תורה ואין טוב אלא תורה (ברכות ה.) ואז נברא הראיה.
records.targetEnglish: The faculty of sight was created primarily for looking into the Torah, for one may not recite the written Torah by heart (Gittin 60b). The first mention of seeing in the Torah concerns the light, in the verse, “God saw the light, that it was good.” Wherever something is mentioned for the first time in the Torah, there lies the root of the matter. Thus it is stated in Bava Kamma 55a concerning the letter tet, which signifies goodness: although tet also occurs in words with the opposite meaning, nevertheless Scripture first used it for good, since from “In the beginning” until “God saw the light, that it was good,” no tet is written. So too with sight: because Scripture first introduces it in connection with the light, as stated above, this is the essential root of sight. The light in this verse refers to the light of Torah, as Genesis Rabbah, chapter 3, says: the five occurrences of “light” in the passage beginning “Let there be light” correspond to the five books of the Torah; and “there is no good other than Torah” (Berakhot 5a). It was then that sight was created.
records.explanation: Here Rav Tzadok tentatively recalls a received rule: a word’s first occurrence reveals the root of its meaning. In his discourse for Rosh Chodesh Tammuz, he states the same rule explicitly and demonstrates its operation. Sight first appears in connection with light; he therefore relates its root to the light of Torah. He also supplies a Talmudic precedent: the discussion in Bava Kamma of tet’s first appearance in tov, “good,” as the basis for its favorable significance in that exposition. This makes the method being applied here to yekar, “preciousness” or “honor,” concrete and connects it to the surrounding discussion of sight and spiritual apprehension. The parallel does not identify the person from whom he received the rule, and preserves his qualification, “it seems to me that I received this teaching.”
